report.summary: One finding: the profile endpoint now returns tax ID and date of birth, sensitive personal data not covered by any information asset in app.tm.hcl.

findings.title: Profile response exposes tax ID and date of birth with no matching information asset

model_excerpt.quote: information_asset "user credentials" classification=Restricted — Usernames and password hashes in the users table

evidence.note: New `TaxID string `json:"tax_id"`` field added to profileResponse struct
New `DateOfBirth string `json:"date_of_birth"`` field added to profileResponse struct
profileHandler now serializes u.TaxID into the GET /profile response body
profileHandler now serializes u.DateOfBirth into the GET /profile response body

relevance.justification: The model's only information asset covers usernames and password hashes; tax ID and date of birth are distinct sensitive personal data now returned over HTTP by the very endpoint the model describes.

findings.agent_prompt: In app.tm.hcl, threat model "login service": the GET /profile response in internal/httpapi/user.go now includes new fields TaxID (`tax_id`) and DateOfBirth (`date_of_birth`), serialized in profileHandler (see internal/httpapi/user.go lines 11-12 and 22-23). The only existing information_asset is "user credentials" (usernames and password hashes), which does not cover this data. Add a new information_asset block — e.g. information_asset "user personal identifiers" with a description covering tax ID and date of birth returned by GET /profile, and classification = "Restricted" (or PII, matching the repo's classification vocabulary). If an existing threat such as "session hijacking" should now reflect the broader impact of a stolen token exposing PII, update its description and impacts accordingly.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an information_asset block in app.tm.hcl covering tax ID and date of birth exposed by GET /profile, and reference it from the session hijacking threat.
